title: The curse on the House of Atreus
lead: Five generations, each paying for the last.

steps.label: Generation I
steps.text: Tantalus serves his son Pelops to the gods. The gods restore the boy; Tantalus is punished forever.

steps.label: Generation II
steps.text: Pelops wins Hippodamia by bribing Myrtilus, then throws him into the sea. Falling, Myrtilus curses Pelops and all his line.

steps.label: Generation III
steps.text: Thyestes seduces his brother’s wife and steals the golden lamb. Atreus feeds Thyestes his own sons, and Thyestes curses the house of Atreus.

steps.label: Generation IV
steps.text: Agamemnon sacrifices Iphigenia to sail for Troy. On his return, Clytemnestra and Aegisthus kill him.

steps.label: Generation V
steps.text: Orestes kills his mother and Aegisthus. Hunted by the Furies, he is tried in Athens and acquitted. The chain breaks.

title: The curse on the House of Labdacus
lead: A crime in Pelops’s house echoes through Thebes.

steps.label: Generation II
steps.text: Laius abducts Chrysippus, the son of Pelops, and Pelops curses him. Only later sources tell this origin.

steps.label: Generation IV
steps.text: An oracle warns Laius that his son will kill him. He has the infant exposed on a mountain.

steps.label: Generation V
steps.text: Grown and unaware, Oedipus kills Laius at a crossroads and marries the widowed queen, his mother. When the truth comes out, Jocasta dies and Oedipus blinds himself.

steps.label: Generation VI
steps.text: Oedipus curses his sons, and they kill each other over Thebes. Antigone buries Polynices against the king’s order and is condemned.

title: The house of Cadmus
lead: A city sown from dragon’s teeth, and a god who came home.

steps.label: The serpent
steps.text: Cadmus comes looking for his sister Europa and founds Thebes instead. He kills the serpent of Ares that guards the spring and, on Athena’s advice, sows its teeth. Armed men spring up and kill each other until five are left.

steps.label: The wedding
steps.text: Cadmus marries Harmonia, daughter of Ares and Aphrodite. The gods come down to the wedding, and the Muses sing.

steps.label: The daughters
steps.text: Harmonia bears Ino, Semele, Agave, Autonoe and a son, Polydorus. Zeus loves Semele, and she dies of it. Her sisters say she lied about her lover.

steps.label: The god comes home
steps.text: Semele’s son Dionysus comes back to Thebes as a god. Agave’s son Pentheus, now king, refuses his rites.

steps.label: The mountain
steps.text: Maddened by the god, Agave and the women of Thebes tear Pentheus apart on Mount Cithaeron. Agave comes home carrying his head, taking it for a beast’s.

steps.label: The serpents
steps.text: Cadmus and Harmonia leave Thebes and are turned into serpents. The throne passes to Polydorus and then to his son Labdacus, whose house the curse will follow.

title: The race for Hippodamia
lead: A king who killed his daughter’s suitors, and the cheat who beat him.

steps.label: The king
steps.text: Oenomaus, king of Pisa and a son of Ares, races his daughter Hippodamia’s suitors in chariots and kills every one who loses.

steps.label: The charioteer
steps.text: Pelops comes to win her. Myrtilus, a son of Hermes and the king’s own charioteer, takes the linchpins out of his master’s chariot, or swaps them for wax, so that Pelops can win. Pindar tells it without a cheat: Poseidon gives Pelops a golden chariot with winged horses.

steps.label: The race
steps.text: Pelops wins the race. Oenomaus dies in the wreck, dragged by his own horses, or in some versions killed by Pelops. Hippodamia becomes the wife of Pelops.

steps.label: The fall
steps.text: Pelops throws Myrtilus into the sea, which is named the Myrtoan Sea after him. The sources give different reasons. Falling, Myrtilus curses Pelops and all his line. For many tellers, the curse on the House of Atreus begins here.

title: The children of Leda
lead: A swan, a goose, an egg, and four famous children.

steps.label: The swan
steps.text: Leda is the wife of Tyndareus, king of Sparta. Zeus comes to her in the form of a swan.

steps.label: The goose
steps.text: The Cypria tells another story. Zeus pursues Nemesis, goddess of retribution, over land and sea, and she turns into a fish and into wild beasts to escape him. In Apollodorus she becomes a goose, and Zeus a swan.

steps.label: Helen
steps.text: Helen is born, a daughter of Zeus. In Euripides she is Leda’s child, hatched from an egg. In the Cypria and Pausanias her mother is Nemesis, and Leda only nurses her. Apollodorus tells both: Helen is Leda’s child, but some say a shepherd found the egg of Nemesis and gave it to Leda, who raised the girl as her own.

steps.label: The twins
steps.text: Leda’s twin sons are Castor and Polydeuces, the Dioscuri. The sources disagree on which of them Zeus fathered. Polydeuces, the immortal twin, gives up half his immortality to share it with his brother.

steps.label: Clytemnestra
steps.text: Their sister Clytemnestra is a daughter of Tyndareus and Leda. She becomes the wife of Agamemnon.

steps.label: The deer
steps.text: Agamemnon kills a deer sacred to Artemis and boasts that he is a better hunter than the goddess. In Aeschylus her anger has another cause: an omen of two eagles tearing apart a pregnant hare.

steps.label: The price
steps.text: Winds hold the Greek fleet at Aulis. Through the seer Calchas, the goddess names her price: Agamemnon’s daughter, Iphigenia.

steps.label: The altar
steps.text: Iphigenia is brought to Aulis with the excuse that she will marry Achilles. Agamemnon sacrifices her so that the fleet can sail for Troy.

steps.label: What the altar saw
steps.text: Here the sources part ways. In Aeschylus she dies at the altar. In the Cypria, Artemis puts a deer in her place, carries her off to the land of the Taurians and makes her immortal. In the Catalogue of Women, where she is called Iphimede, Artemis makes her immortal; Pausanias reports that Hesiod made her Hecate. In Euripides, Artemis puts a deer in her place and takes her to the Taurians to serve as her priestess.

steps.label: The mother
steps.text: Clytemnestra avenges her daughter. When Agamemnon comes home from Troy, she kills him. In Homer, Aegisthus strikes the blow, and the sacrifice is never mentioned.

title: Perseus and the Gorgon
lead: A shower of gold, a chest at sea, a head that turns men to stone.

steps.label: The oracle
steps.text: Acrisius, king of Argos, has only a daughter, Danaë. An oracle tells him that her son will kill him. He shuts her away in a bronze chamber under the earth; in Hyginus, behind a stone wall.

steps.label: The shower of gold
steps.text: Zeus comes to her as a shower of gold, and she bears Perseus. Apollodorus adds that some named Proetus, Acrisius’ brother, as the father. Acrisius will not believe in Zeus. He shuts mother and child in a wooden chest and casts it into the sea.

steps.label: Seriphos
steps.text: The chest washes up on Seriphos, and a fisherman, Dictys, takes them in. His brother Polydectes, the king, wants Danaë, but her son is now a man. Polydectes asks his friends for horses as gifts. Perseus says he would not refuse even the Gorgon’s head, and the king takes him at his word.

steps.label: The Graeae
steps.text: Led by Hermes and Athena, Perseus comes to the Graeae, three old sisters who share one eye and one tooth. He snatches the eye as it passes between them and gives it back only when they show him the way to the nymphs. The nymphs give him winged sandals, a pouch and the cap of Hades, which makes him unseen; Hermes gives him a sickle.

steps.label: Medusa
steps.text: Of the three Gorgons only Medusa is mortal. Perseus finds them asleep and, looking only at her reflection in a bronze shield, cuts off her head while Athena guides his hand. Pegasus and Chrysaor, her children by Poseidon, spring from her neck. Her sisters wake and give chase, but the cap hides him. Ovid tells why she looked as she did: Poseidon lay with her in Athena’s temple, and Athena turned her hair to snakes.

steps.label: Atlas
steps.text: Ovid alone tells this. Perseus asks the Titan Atlas for a night’s shelter. Atlas, warned that a son of Zeus would rob his golden apples, drives him off. Perseus holds up the head, and Atlas becomes a mountain, his beard and hair forests, his bones rock.

steps.label: Andromeda
steps.text: In Ethiopia, Queen Cassiopeia has boasted that she is more beautiful than the Nereids; in Hyginus she says it of her daughter. Poseidon sends a sea monster. The oracle of Ammon says the land will be saved if Andromeda, the king’s daughter, is given to it, and Cepheus chains her to a rock. Perseus kills the monster and claims her as his wife.

steps.label: The wedding
steps.text: Andromeda was promised first to Phineus, Cepheus’ brother. He plots against Perseus, or, in Ovid, storms the wedding feast with his men. Perseus holds up the Gorgon’s head, and they turn to stone.

steps.label: The return
steps.text: Back on Seriphos, Perseus finds his mother and Dictys hiding at the altars from Polydectes. He walks into the king’s hall and shows the head: Polydectes and his guests turn to stone. Perseus makes Dictys king, gives the sandals, the pouch and the cap back to Hermes, and gives the head to Athena, who sets it on her shield.

steps.label: The discus
steps.text: Acrisius, fearing the oracle, flees to Larissa. Perseus follows him there and joins the games. His discus strikes Acrisius and kills him: in Apollodorus it hits his foot, in Hyginus his head. The oracle comes true.

title: The labours of Heracles
lead: Twelve labours, one jealous goddess, and a robe soaked in poison.

steps.label: Two births
steps.text: Zeus comes to Alcmene in the shape of her husband Amphitryon, and she conceives Heracles. On the day he is due, Zeus swears that a child of his blood born that day will rule all around him. Hera holds back Alcmene’s labour and hurries the birth of Eurystheus, a grandson of Perseus, so he is born first and Heracles must serve him. When the baby is eight months old, Hera sends two serpents to his cradle, and he strangles them.

steps.label: The madness
steps.text: Heracles marries Megara, daughter of Creon of Thebes. Hera drives him mad, and he kills their children. The oracle at Delphi sends him to Tiryns to serve Eurystheus and do the labours he sets; then he will be immortal. In Euripides the madness comes after the labours, and Megara dies with her sons.

steps.label: The lion
steps.text: First Eurystheus asks for the hide of the Nemean Lion, which no weapon can pierce. Heracles drives it into its cave, which has two mouths, blocks one, and chokes the lion with his arms. From then on he wears its skin. Eurystheus is so frightened that he has a bronze jar made to hide in, and gives his orders through a herald.

steps.label: The Hydra
steps.text: At Lerna lives the Hydra, with nine heads, one of them immortal. For every head Heracles cuts off, two grow back, and Hera sends a crab to bite his foot. His nephew Iolaus burns each neck as it is cut, so nothing grows. Heracles buries the immortal head under a rock and dips his arrows in the venom. Eurystheus will not count this labour: Heracles had help.

steps.label: Hind, boar, stables, birds
steps.text: He brings back alive the golden-horned hind of Ceryneia, sacred to Artemis, and the boar of Erymanthus. He cleans the stables of Augeas in a day by turning the rivers Alpheus and Peneus through them, but Augeas refuses to pay, and Eurystheus refuses to count it. With bronze rattles from Athena he scares the birds off the lake of Stymphalus and shoots them. Years later he comes back to Elis and kills Augeas.

steps.label: The bull and the mares
steps.text: From Crete he brings the bull that Minos would not sacrifice. In Thrace he kills King Diomedes, a son of Ares, and drives off his mares, which eat human flesh. In Euripides he stops on the way at the house of Admetus, whose wife Alcestis has just died for him, wrestles Death at her tomb and brings her back.

steps.label: The belt
steps.text: Eurystheus’ daughter wants the belt of Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons. Hippolyta agrees to give it, but Hera, disguised as an Amazon, tells the women their queen is being carried off. In the fighting Heracles kills Hippolyta and takes the belt. Sailing home past Troy, he saves King Laomedon’s daughter Hesione from a sea monster, and Laomedon cheats him of the reward.

steps.label: Geryon
steps.text: He crosses the Ocean in the golden cup of the Sun to the island of Erytheia, far in the west. There he kills the dog Orthus, the herdsman Eurytion and Geryon, who has three bodies, and drives the red cattle back to Greece.

steps.label: The golden apples
steps.text: Next he must bring the golden apples of the Hesperides, guarded by a serpent. In Apollodorus he holds up the sky while Atlas fetches them. Atlas offers to take the apples to Eurystheus himself; Heracles asks him to hold the sky a moment while he puts a pad on his head, and walks away with the apples. In Euripides he kills the serpent and picks them himself.

steps.label: Cerberus
steps.text: Last, he must bring Cerberus up from the land of the dead. Hades lets him take the dog if he can master it without weapons. Heracles wrestles it into submission, frees Theseus from the chair of forgetfulness, shows Cerberus to Eurystheus, and takes it back.

steps.label: Nessus
steps.text: Free at last, Heracles wins Deianira, daughter of Oeneus, by wrestling the river Achelous. At the river Evenus the centaur Nessus carries her across and tries to rape her, and Heracles shoots him with an arrow dipped in the Hydra’s poison. Dying, Nessus tells Deianira to keep his blood as a charm to win back her husband’s love.

steps.label: The robe
steps.text: Years later Heracles sacks Oechalia and sends home the princess Iole. Afraid of losing him, Deianira smears a robe with the blood of Nessus and sends it to him. The poison burns into his flesh. He has himself laid on a pyre on Mount Oeta, and Poeas, or his son Philoctetes, lights it. Heracles is taken up to Olympus, reconciled with Hera, and marries her daughter Hebe.

title: Theseus and the Minotaur
lead: A sword under a rock, a ball of thread, and a sail that was never changed.

steps.label: Two fathers
steps.text: Aegeus, king of Athens, has no son. On his way home from Delphi he stops at Troezen, and its king makes him drunk and puts him to bed with his daughter Aethra. The same night Poseidon lies with her. Before he leaves, Aegeus hides his sword and sandals under a great rock: when the boy can lift it, he is to come to Athens.

steps.label: The road
steps.text: Grown, Theseus lifts the rock and takes the sword and sandals. He goes to Athens by land, though the road is full of robbers, and kills them one by one: Periphetes and his club, Sinis the pine-bender, Sciron who kicked travellers off a cliff, Cercyon the wrestler, and Procrustes with his bed.

steps.label: The cup
steps.text: In Athens, Aegeus has married Medea, who has fled from Corinth. She knows who the stranger is. She persuades Aegeus to send him against the bull of Marathon, and when he comes back alive, to give him poison at a feast. As Theseus draws his sword to cut the meat, Aegeus knows it, and dashes the cup from his hand. Medea flees.

steps.label: The tribute
steps.text: Minos of Crete has lost his son Androgeus in Attica: some say Aegeus sent him against the bull of Marathon, others that he was ambushed on the road. Minos makes war on Athens, and Athens must send seven youths and seven girls to Crete, to be fed to the Minotaur.

steps.label: The Minotaur
steps.text: The Minotaur, with a bull’s head on a man’s body, is the son of Minos’ queen Pasiphae. Minos would not sacrifice the bull Poseidon sent him from the sea, and Poseidon made Pasiphae love it. Daedalus built her a wooden cow, and then the Labyrinth to hide her child.

steps.label: The thread
steps.text: Theseus sails to Crete among the fourteen. Ariadne, Minos’ daughter, falls in love with him and, on Daedalus’ advice, gives him a ball of thread. He ties it at the door, finds the Minotaur at the heart of the Labyrinth, kills it, in Apollodorus with his fists, and follows the thread out.

steps.label: Naxos
steps.text: He sails away with Ariadne and the children, and leaves her on the island of Naxos, called Dia. Dionysus finds her there and makes her his wife. The Odyssey tells it darker: Artemis killed her on Dia, on the word of Dionysus.

steps.label: The black sail
steps.text: Theseus had promised his father a white sail if he came home alive. He forgets, and the ship comes in under black. Aegeus, watching from the Acropolis, thinks his son is dead and throws himself down. Theseus becomes king of Athens.

title: Jason and the Golden Fleece
lead: A ram of gold, a man with one sandal, and a princess who gave up everything for him.

steps.label: The golden ram
steps.text: Athamas, a king in Boeotia, has two children by the cloud Nephele, Phrixus and Helle. Then he marries Ino, daughter of Cadmus. Ino parches the seed corn so that nothing grows, and bribes the messengers from Delphi to say the god wants Phrixus sacrificed. At the altar, Nephele sends a ram with a golden fleece, and it flies off with both children. Helle falls into the sea, which is called the Hellespont after her. Phrixus reaches Colchis, sacrifices the ram to Zeus, and gives its fleece to King Aeetes, who nails it to an oak in the grove of Ares.

steps.label: One sandal
steps.text: In Iolcus, Pelias has taken the throne from his half-brother Aeson. An oracle has told him to beware a man with one sandal. Aeson’s son Jason, raised by the centaur Chiron, comes down to a sacrifice and loses a sandal crossing a river. Pelias sees him, and sends him to bring back the Golden Fleece. In Pindar, Jason comes to claim the throne, and Pelias says he will give it up for the fleece.

steps.label: The Argo
steps.text: Argus builds a ship of fifty oars, the Argo, with Athena’s help, and the best men of Greece sail in her: Heracles, Castor and Polydeuces, the singer Orpheus, the sons of the North Wind. Their first landfall is Lemnos, where the women have killed all their men. Only Queen Hypsipyle has saved her father. The Argonauts stay with the women, and Jason has sons by the queen.

steps.label: Hylas
steps.text: In Mysia, Heracles’ young lover Hylas goes to fetch water. The nymphs of the spring fall in love with him and draw him down into it. Heracles searches for him all night, and the Argo sails without them.

steps.label: The Harpies
steps.text: In Thrace lives the blind seer Phineus. Whenever food is set before him, the Harpies swoop down, snatch it, and foul what they leave. The sons of the North Wind chase them off. In return Phineus tells the Argonauts how to pass the Clashing Rocks: let a dove fly through first. The rocks close on its tail feathers, open again, and the Argo rows through with only the tip of her stern torn away.

steps.label: The bulls
steps.text: In Colchis, Aeetes promises the fleece if Jason can yoke his two bronze-footed, fire-breathing bulls, plough a field, and sow it with a dragon’s teeth. His daughter Medea, a witch and a priestess of Hecate, falls in love with Jason. She makes him swear to marry her and gives him a salve that keeps off fire and iron. He yokes the bulls. Armed men spring up from the teeth; he throws a stone among them, and they kill each other.

steps.label: The fleece
steps.text: Aeetes will not keep his word, and means to burn the ship. At night Medea leads Jason to the grove where a serpent that never sleeps guards the fleece. She lulls it to sleep with her drugs, and Jason takes the fleece. In Pindar and Hyginus he kills the serpent; in Euripides Medea does.

steps.label: Absyrtus
steps.text: Medea flees on the Argo, taking her young brother Absyrtus. When her father’s ship comes close, she kills the boy, cuts him in pieces, and throws them into the sea. Aeetes stops to gather his son’s limbs, and the Argo gets away. Zeus is angry at the murder, and Circe, Medea’s aunt, cleanses them of the blood.

steps.label: The man of bronze
steps.text: Off Crete, the bronze giant Talos guards the island, throwing rocks at every ship. He has one vein, running from his neck to his ankle, stopped with a nail. Medea drives him mad with her drugs, or tricks him with a promise to make him immortal, and pulls out the nail. His ichor runs out, and he dies.

steps.label: The cauldron
steps.text: In Iolcus, Pelias has driven Aeson to his death, and Jason gives the fleece to his uncle. Medea cuts up an old ram, boils it with herbs, and a lamb leaps out of the pot. She tells Pelias’ daughters that their father can be made young the same way. They cut him up and boil him, and he does not come out. In Ovid, Aeson is still alive, and Medea makes him young again.

steps.label: Corinth
steps.text: Driven out of Iolcus, Jason and Medea live ten years in Corinth. Then Jason leaves her to marry Glauce, the king’s daughter. Medea sends the bride a robe and a golden crown. When she puts them on, they burn her, and her father Creon with her. Medea kills her own sons by Jason and escapes in a chariot drawn by winged serpents, the gift of her grandfather the Sun.
